title: Product photography for a clothing label
excerpt: Photograph cloth, fit, and the body with one crop and one light. A grid of unrelated frames makes the label look unfinished.
alt: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it. Garment frames should be as consistent as a single desk, not a new set for every piece.
caption: One desk, one setup, the same for the whole line. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Which frame should be the thumbnail for a garment?
faqs.answer: The on-body crop the whole line shares, usually full enough to judge length. Detail macros and campaign scenes can live on the product page. If one tile is a face crop and the next is a full figure, the category will look unfinished.

faqs.question: How do you keep color honest across a colorway?
faqs.answer: Shoot the colors together, in the same pose and light, and compare the files to the cloth on a phone. A different concept per color compares the pose, not the dye. You will not control every screen. You can avoid publishing a different garment.

faqs.question: What makes clothing images hurt the page?
faqs.answer: Files that are far larger than the template, or that load without reserved space, so the price jumps. Google's Core Web Vitals ask for the largest content to appear within two and a half seconds and for layout shift to stay very small. Export the size you display, and keep size charts in text, not burned into the photo.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
A clothing label product photography setup has to show cloth, fit, and the garment on a body, with a crop and a background the whole line can share. The buyer is deciding whether this piece will work on them. A grid of unrelated crops looks like an unfinished shop, even when every garment is well made.

Photograph the cloth and the person in a system. Use the same light and the same margin. Let storytelling frames stay off the thumbnail unless every thumbnail is a story, which is a harder system to keep.

## The set each garment needs

Decide the set by the form, then repeat it.

- An on-body hero, full enough to judge length and fit, cropped like the rest of the line.
- A second angle that answers the question the hero hides: back, side, or walking, if the cloth moves.
- A detail of fabric, stitch, or hardware, in the same light.
- A flat or ghost view only if your buyers use it to judge cut. If you include it, include it for the line, not for one difficult jacket.

State height and size worn in the page text, and keep the model's presentation consistent enough that fit is comparable. Changing from a close crop of a face to a distant full-body across one category makes the clothes look like they come from different labels. Pick full-body for the thumbnail if length matters, which it usually does, and do not mix in a beauty crop as a neighboring tile.

If you shoot on more than one model, do not change the camera distance between them. A taller person filling the frame and a shorter person floating in it is a mixed crop. Adjust who stands where, not the focal length, so the garments occupy the same portion of the frame.

Colorways of one style are the same shot repeated, not a new concept per color. The buyer is comparing navy with brown. A different pose per color compares the pose.

## Light, cloth, and color that tell the truth

Cloth is the product. Side light that reveals a twill, and a fill that does not kill it, will do more than a complicated set. Shiny linings and matte wools need the same session logic so a jacket and its lining do not look like two eras of the brand.

Watch clipping on white shirts and black coats. A white that blows out has no cloth. A black that closes up has no seam. Expose for the fabric, not for a dramatic background. The background should be quieter than the garment. A busy interior that fights a print is a portrait of the room.

Match color to the sample in the hand, on a screen your customer might use. If the red is hotter in the file than on the table, correct it before upload. You will not remove every phone's shift. You can avoid publishing a different garment. Shoot the whole colorway together so the relationship between colors stays honest.

Movement shots are optional and expensive to keep consistent. If the label depends on drape, one walking frame in the same crop is worth more than ten campaign images you cannot repeat next season. If you cannot repeat it, it does not belong in the grid.

## Background and crop are the grid

Choose one background family for heroes. Seamless paper, a plain wall, a single studio corner. Use it until you deliberately change the whole catalog. A beach, a bedroom, and a white sweep in one row of products is the unfinished look. Campaign images can live on the homepage or a journal. The category thumbnail stays in the system.

Set the margin. The head may crop out if the system is about the clothes, or the full figure may stay if length is the point. Write that down. "Sometimes we crop at the eyes" is how the next shoot drifts. Align the feet or the shoulders across the set so the grid has a horizon. Without a horizon, every tile jitters and the shop feels accidental.

Props should not cover the hem, the waistband, or the closure. A bag in front of a trouser is a picture of a bag. Hands in pockets are fine if the silhouette stays clear and you are consistent. One style with arms up and the next with arms crossed will look like a mistake in the template even when both photos are good.

Check the heroes in the real grid at phone size before you approve the set. A detail that felt precious on a large monitor may be a muddy square on the thumbnail. If it does not read small, it is not the hero. Swap in the full-body frame.

## Speed, shift, and words on the image

These files are large and they are the main event on the page, so they decide whether the garment appears quickly and whether the layout jumps. Google's [Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) targets are Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint under 200 milliseconds, and Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. Export the display size. Give the template a reserved ratio so the price does not leap down when the image arrives. A layout jump on a size selector is how people tap the wrong size.

Do not burn size charts, prices, or slogans into the photograph. The [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) wants a text alternative that describes the image, and it wants the real text to live as text. Alt can be "Wool coat, knee length, worn by a model, front view." The fiber and the measurements belong in the page, where they can be updated and read. A JPEG is a bad place to keep a size guide. When the pattern changes, you would have to reshoot the words.

Name files by style, color, and view. The person uploading the drop at midnight should not have to guess which frame is the back. A consistent name is part of the photography, because the wrong back view on the front hero is a fit lie.

## What to reshoot, and what to stop styling

Lay the line up and look for the odd one: warmer light, tighter crop, different horizon. Fix that frame. One odd tile dominates a small grid. On a large marketplace nobody notices. On a label's own shop, it is the first thing a careful buyer feels, even if they cannot name it.

Reshoot if the garment sample changed. Do not keep last season's photographs for a recut with a new length. The photograph is a specification. A mismatched spec creates returns you will blame on the customer.

Stop adding a new location for every drop if you cannot reshoot the existing line. A half-new grid is worse than a plain one. Plan the change between seasons, and budget the reshoot as part of the change. Until then, hold the old system. Consistency beats a better idea you only applied to the newest four styles.

If a piece wrinkles in a way you would steam before a wholesale appointment, steam it before the shutter. Publishing the wrinkle you would not show a buyer in person is a different brand from the one you run offline. Texture that is part of the cloth stays. A shipping crease does not.

Hanabi's [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) includes brand and ecommerce projects where the pictures and the template had to agree. Bring a grid, not a single hero, if you want to see where a line is drifting.

## Dark cloth, light cloth, and print

Black and white garments are where small labels lose the product. Bracket the exposure on purpose, and keep the one frame where the seam and the button still exist. If you publish the moodier frame because it looks expensive, you have hidden the design. The expensive look can be a second image. The hero has to survive a phone in daylight.

Prints and stripes need to sit straight in the frame, or the buyer will think the garment is twisted. Spend the minute on the stand or the model's stance. A print that moirés or changes scale because you moved closer is another mixed-crop problem. Keep the camera distance you wrote down.

Sheer fabrics need a background that does not turn them into a different color. If the nude sweep shows through and shifts the cloth, switch to the background you use for the rest of the line or accept that this piece is shot on a body only. Do not invent a third background for one blouse and then drop it into the grid.

Hang and steam, then wait a minute before shooting so the cloth settles. A frame grabbed while someone is still pinning will show the pin. The contact sheet will not save you if every frame has a clip at the hem.

## Direction for the next drop

Write a one-page direction: background, crop, horizon, the frame set, export size, alt pattern, and how colorways repeat. The photographer can change. The page should not. Review it when you add a form you have not shot before, such as a hat or a shoe, and give that form its own row instead of forcing the coat crop onto it.

On shoot day, capture the set in order, style by style, and do not leave the detail frame for "later" on a different setup. Later is how light drifts. A contact sheet with the rejects marked "crop," "clip," or "color" is how the next photographer stays inside the system.

Keep the original files. You will need a different export when the template changes its ratio. Cropping from a too-small JPEG is how margins collapse and the horizon dies. The direction includes the master frame, not only the shop export.

Food is a different subject and the same grid problem. [An online shop for a food brand](/blog/an-online-shop-for-a-food-brand) comes next, because taste cannot be clicked, so the pack and the story have to do the work the cloth just did.
